error.signature: AI tells a traveler that riding as a passenger on a Kenyan boda boda (motorcycle taxi) without a helmet is legal since it is common local practice

verdict.summary: The National Transport and Safety Authority (Operation of Motorcycles) Regulations, 2015 require every motorcycle owner to supply two KEBS-standard helmets and two reflective jackets bearing the registration number - one set for the rider, one for the passenger - and require both rider and passenger to wear them. Contravening the regulations carries a fine of up to KES 20,000, imprisonment of up to six months, or both. In practice most boda boda operators do not carry a spare helmet, but that widespread non-compliance does not make riding bare-headed as a passenger legal, and it is not a safe assumption for a visitor to copy.

dead_ends.action: Tell a visitor that going without a helmet as a boda boda passenger is fine in Kenya because it is what most local riders and passengers actually do
dead_ends.why_fails: Kenya Law's consolidated text of the National Transport and Safety Authority (Operation of Motorcycles) Regulations, 2015 requires the owner to 'provide the rider and passenger with the protective gear stipulated in regulation 4(1)' - two KEBS-standard helmets and two reflective jackets - and sets a general penalty under Regulation 15 of a fine not exceeding twenty thousand shillings, imprisonment for up to six months, or both, for contravening the regulations. Common practice ignoring the rule does not change what the law requires.
dead_ends.condition: Boda boda passenger travel anywhere in Kenya
dead_ends.common_misconception: That a rule ignored by most riders in practice must not really be in force, or does not apply to passengers as well as riders.

dead_ends.action: Treat the existence of the helmet law as evidence that Kenyan boda boda passengers are actually protected in practice
dead_ends.why_fails: WHO's Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023 Kenya country profile records that the national helmet law applies to both drivers and passengers, yet real observed wearing rates in some Kenyan districts were below one-third for drivers and under 2% for passengers - the law existing is not evidence that a given operator will actually have or offer a passenger helmet.
dead_ends.condition: Assessing real-world passenger safety, not just legal requirements

workarounds.action: Before boarding, ask the rider for the passenger helmet the regulations require them to carry; if they do not have one, treat that as a signal the operator is already non-compliant and prefer a licensed taxi, ride-hailing car, or a different boda boda operator who carries proper gear
